structure.title: 6. What Explains the Absence of a Spending Response?

observations.statement: The design is an information provision experiment embedded in a bank phone survey; all respondents receive at least one macro signal (no pure control), which the authors justify by citing prior designs and using it to measure cross-learning explicitly.

The learning specification interacts the signal-minus-prior gap with random treatment assignment, and the non-interacted gap term is included to absorb spurious reversion toward the signal; the interaction coefficient is named as the true learning rate.

The reduced-form spending regressions are labelled intention-to-treat; a treatment-on-the-treated effect is obtained by a two-endogenous-variable IV model where belief updates are instrumented with the two information shocks, following prior information experiments.

Experimenter demand is addressed by design: unincentivized posterior elicitation, callers presented as university researchers rather than bank staff, neutral wording, and a comparison of updating between the phone experiment and an online follow-up.
observations.locator: Section 3.3, Elicitation of posterior beliefs, footnotes 14 and 15

observations.statement: The order of the two prior-belief questions is randomized so that neither variable is made more salient, and the order of information feedback follows the same randomized order.
observations.locator: Section 3.3, Elicitation of prior beliefs; footnote 12

observations.statement: A stylized intertemporal choice model with durable/tradable goods yields three propositions that map one-to-one onto the outcome columns of the main table; proofs are relegated to an appendix and a CRRA extension to the Internet Appendix.

Unit is an individual credit card customer of one Malaysian bank; survey responses are linked to the bank's administrative transaction records covering months before and after the intervention; the fieldwork window is stated by month and year.

Partially completed surveys are dropped, with a statement that missingness after the information stage cannot be rejected as random; respondents with extreme exchange rate priors are excluded because the survey system truncated their answers, and the authors note they would trim such outliers anyway following expectations literature.

The sample frame was requested from the bank restricted to recently opened accounts; a random subset was invited; call center operators received randomized daily call lists and were instructed to make at least one follow-up attempt.

Nonresponse is characterised by comparing respondents with a bank-provided random sample of invited nonrespondents on administrative demographics and pre-treatment spending, with equality-of-means p-values in a dedicated table.
Every regression and descriptive table reports the number of observations; the survey experiment tables show smaller samples for heterogeneity panels and asset-demand arms.
Debit card transactions are deliberately not collected because pre-intervention summary data showed they are a negligible share of spending.

The information shock is defined as the signal-minus-prior gap multiplied by a treatment indicator; the same two shock variables serve as regressors in reduced forms and as excluded instruments in the IV model.

Spending outcomes are monthly averages over the post-treatment window to reduce outlier and seasonality concerns; debt repayment is measured over the same window; pre-treatment spending in the same category enters as a control.

Transactions are classified by Merchant Category Code: durable versus nondurable follows literature categorizations, while tradable versus nontradable is a new manual classification of each MCC using the standard definition, with services assigned to nontradable.

Self-reported spending plans and economic outlook questions are coded on a three-point scale (minus one, zero, plus one), with wording modeled on the Michigan Survey and the NY Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations.
All monetary amounts are converted from local currency to US dollars at a fixed exchange rate on a stated reference date.

Signals are expert consensus forecasts from named public forecast websites, updated once during fieldwork for a quarterly revision; historical forecast accuracy is documented in an Internet Appendix figure.

Main tables report N, R-squared, outcome mean, median and standard deviation beneath each column; notes list all controls and fixed effects (week and surveyor) and state that robust standard errors are in parentheses.

A single fixed set of controls is used in every regression in the paper (demographics, log income, week and surveyor fixed effects, plus pre-treatment spending for spending outcomes); the authors say controls should not move point estimates under randomization but improve power.
observations.quote: We use the same set of standard controls in all regressions presented in this paper

observations.statement: The IV and OLS tables print confidence intervals in brackets under each coefficient, and the IV table reports a Kleibergen-Paap F-statistic per endogenous variable and column.

Belief-update and spending regressions share an identical right-hand side; the same table holds both survey-data belief columns and transaction-data spending columns, and a later table repeats the layout with self-reported plans as outcomes.

Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are used throughout at the individual level; no discussion of clustering appears, consistent with individual-level randomization, but the choice is not explicitly justified.

Because the first stage for one endogenous variable is weak, Anderson-Rubin confidence intervals are used for the IV estimates and tF confidence intervals (Lee et al.) are added in the Internet Appendix; the authors caution that those upper bounds be read carefully.
observations.locator: Section 5.4, Table 4 notes, Internet Appendix Table IA.5

observations.statement: One imbalanced covariate among eleven is described as expected by chance at the ten percent level, and it is nonetheless included as a control in all regressions as standard practice.
A randomization balance table shows demographics, pre-treatment spending and prior beliefs by treatment arm with joint-test p-values and per-arm F-statistics, with robust standard errors of the mean.

The belief-update regressions in the main reduced-form table function as the first stage; Kleibergen-Paap F-statistics are reported in the IV table and a weak instrument for one variable is acknowledged in text.
Before regressions, a binned scatterplot of belief update against potential update is shown separately for treated and control groups, with the difference in slopes interpreted as the learning rate.
Distributions of prior beliefs are plotted as histograms with the expert forecast marked by a dashed line before treatment effects are presented.
Effects on general economic outlook and personal financial situation are reported in the Internet Appendix as a check that treatments do not operate through optimism or pessimism.

Main results are re-estimated restricting to observations where the two shock distributions have common support, to make inflation and exchange rate effects comparable; reported in the Internet Appendix.

Reduced-form, IV and plain OLS versions of the spending regressions are presented as three consecutive main-text tables, with the OLS using full variation in expectations framed as a precision-versus-identification trade-off.
Treatment effects at a shorter one-month horizon are reported in the Internet Appendix to check persistence of the information effect.

Heterogeneity by income, by salaried versus self-employed status, by transportation-worker occupation identified from transaction data, and by baseline foreign currency spending is reported in Internet Appendix tables and discussed in text as mechanism evidence.
observations.locator: Sections 5.3 and 6.2, Internet Appendix Tables IA.4, IA.6 to IA.8

observations.statement: In the supplementary survey experiment, heterogeneity by above-median financial literacy is reported as an interaction term in a second panel of the main-text tables.
Income heterogeneity is described as suggestive and the lack of significance is attributed to sample size and income homogeneity among card holders.

Null results are interpreted through upper bounds of confidence intervals expressed in dollars, in standard deviations of the outcome, and as a share of the outcome median; the induced shift in expectations is also expressed in standard deviations.
Learning rates are benchmarked against a survey of information experiments and against specific prior studies, with differences attributed to population and survey mode.
A divergence from contemporaneous work on total spending is discussed and attributed to differences in how spending is measured (scanner panel versus passive card records).

A separate mental model survey experiment with randomized hypothetical scenarios, a fixed-nominal-income arm, demand for indexed assets and a financial literacy module is used to support one mechanism, and four alternatives are each tested and ruled out in named subsections.
Self-reported spending plans elicited immediately after treatment are used as an intermediate outcome to distinguish time inconsistency from absence of intention.

Salience is tested by estimating effects separately for large and small transactions defined by pre-treatment quartile cutoffs and by high-ticket spending categories, with normalized spending variables.
observations.locator: Section 6.3 Salience, Internet Appendix Tables IA.9 and IA.10

observations.statement: The authors state that credit card customers are not representative of the population and compare sample demographics and income with national statistics.

The authors acknowledge that small effects cannot be ruled out, that exchange rate IV bounds rest on a weak first stage, and that occupational heterogeneity cannot be statistically distinguished because one group is small.
The model's log-log utility is flagged as unable to capture income effects, with a more general case shown to be sign-ambiguous in the Internet Appendix.

The setting is argued to be informative because the two macro variables differ in salience, documented with Google Trends and newspaper counts, and the affluent card-holder sample is framed as the population most likely to respond.
Tables use three-level significance stars, notes define every variable and control, and two summary statistics tables precede results; the Internet Appendix tables are numbered IA.n.
The composition of spending across durable, tradable and uncategorized groups is shown as a grid of squares each representing an equal share of spending.
The first figure is a schematic of treatment conditions and the experiment timeline; background figures show macro time series and public interest measures before any results.

The introduction previews three findings and lists alternative mechanisms rejected; theory precedes background, design precedes data, main results precede a separate mechanisms section, and there is no roadmap paragraph.

Heterogeneity, placebo outcomes, horizon checks, tF intervals and the survey instrument are all placed in an Internet Appendix, with the main text summarizing each in one or two sentences; no separate robustness section exists.
A dedicated data subsection correlates self-reported spending plans with realized administrative spending to motivate the use of administrative outcomes.
A one-sentence statement before the references gives a Harvard Dataverse DOI for replication code and data; no software is named in the text.

Administrative transaction and demographic data were shared anonymized by a partner bank for respondents and a sample of nonrespondents; survey data were collected by the research team through the bank's outreach program.
Public interest measures come from Google Trends and a newspaper archive; macro series come from FRED; forecasts from Statista and Trading Economics.
IRB approval and an AEA RCT registry number are given in the title footnote; verbal opt-in consent is described and the absence of written consent is explained by data anonymization.
Survey wording was adapted through qualitative interviews and an online pilot before fieldwork; the full instrument is in the Internet Appendix.
